domains.title: She-Who-Invites
domains.subtitle: Creator Goddess, Mother of Kami, Queen of Yomi
domains.lead: Izanami is the female half of the primordial creator pair and the first being to die. Her body became the landscape of the underworld, and her exchange of curses with Izanagi across the sealed slope set the arithmetic of mortality. She is both the mother of the gods and the fearsome queen of Yomi.

cards.name: Creator Goddess
cards.desc: With Izanagi, she stirred the ocean with the jeweled spear and bore the eight great islands.

cards.name: Mother of Kami
cards.desc: She gave birth to the elemental gods, the land, the sea, and the winds.

cards.name: Death in Childbirth
cards.desc: She died bearing the fire god Kagutsuchi; her dying body birthed the thunders.

cards.name: Queen of Yomi
cards.desc: Beyond the boulder she rules the dead and sends the thunders forth.

symbols.name: The comb
symbols.meaning: Her own comb's tooth, lit by Izanagi, revealed her decay — the light that ended their marriage

symbols.name: Boulder of Yomotsu-hirasaka
symbols.meaning: The stone she cannot cross; the sealed door between the living and the dead

symbols.name: Fire (Kagutsuchi)
symbols.meaning: The child that killed her — and the ancestor of every hearth

symbols.name: The eight thunders
symbols.meaning: Yakusanoikazuchi, born from her head, breast, belly, loins, hands, and feet — her honor guard in Yomi

symbols.name: Mount Hiba
symbols.meaning: Her burial place in the land of Kibi, where the myth touches real geography

mythology.lead: Izanami's mythology is central to Japanese understandings of creation, death, and the boundary between the living and the dead — and it never forgives her for speaking first at the pillar.

myths.title: She Who Stirred the Brine
myths.text: The heavenly kami gave the command to the pair, but it was Izanami who set her hand on the spear. Standing upon the Floating Bridge of Heaven, she and Izanagi lowered the jeweled Ame-no-Nuboko into the formless ocean and stirred; the brine dripping from its tip congealed into Onogoroshima, and upon that first island the couple founded their union and their hall (Kojiki 1). The chronicles, even while making her the mother of everything, mark her as the one who stepped outside the ritual order — she spoke the first greeting at the pillar — and who suffered for it. Everything that follows, islands, gods, death, night, proceeds from her equal hand on the spear. The creation is a marriage as much as a manufacture: the world begins in a couple's shared labor, and its first law is how they address each other.

myths.title: Hiruko, the Leech-Child
myths.text: When the couple circled the heavenly pillar to greet each other and beget, Izanami spoke first; their firstborn, Hiruko, was a boneless child who could not stand even at the age of three, and they set him adrift in a reed boat (Kojiki 1). Consulting the heavenly kami, they learned the error — the man's voice must come first — and repeated the rite in the proper order; Izanami then bore the eight great islands and the gods of wind, river, sea, and mountain. Modern readers have reclaimed Hiruko as a poignant emblem, the 'sun-child' as the name can be parsed, the disabled firstborn of the gods; some traditions even drifted to connect the drifting child with Ebisu. But the chronicle records him only as the price of a word out of place. For Izanami the myth is a double wound: blamed for the error, she is then consumed bearing the children that redeem it.

myths.title: Death by the Fire Child
myths.text: Her last birth was Kagutsuchi, the fire god. The child burned her as he was born, and Izanami lay dying, her lower body seared. Even in death the creation did not stop: from her vomit came the mountain-smith Kanayamahiko, from her excrement the clay-god Haniyasu, from her urine the water-goddess Mitsuhanome — and from her head, breast, belly, loins, left and right hands and feet came the eight thunder deities, Yakusanoikazuchi, who would one day guard her in Yomi (Kojiki 1). She named the mountain of her burial before she died: Mount Hiba, in the land of Kibi. The passage is the Kojiki at its most elemental: the mother of everything dies of her most brilliant child, and her dying body, catalogued organ by organ, becomes the map of the underworld she is about to rule.

myths.title: One Thousand, One Thousand Five Hundred
myths.text: In Yomi, when Izanagi broke his promise and lit the comb, Izanami — maggot-crowned, thunder-fleshed — cried that he had shamed her, and sent the hags and the eight thunders after him. He escaped to the slope of Yomotsu-hirasaka and rolled the great boulder into the pass between them. Then the dead queen pronounced the verdict that still governs the world: each day, she said, I will strangle a thousand of the people of your land. From the other side of the stone Izanagi answered: then each day I will cause fifteen hundred to be born (Kojiki 1). Her curse is not repealed but outpaced — death legislated in daily arithmetic, answered by a larger birthrate. The exchange is Japan's theodicy in a single statistic: the grave wins every skirmish and loses the census.

lore.syncretism: Izanami's Buddhist reception was quieter than her consort's: as queen of Yomi she was overlaid on images of the underworld's judges and on the earth deities of esoteric cosmology, and in some medieval systems Yomi itself was mapped onto the realm of hungry ghosts. Her gendered fate — the first mother, the first corpse — made her a natural figure for funerary reflection, though no stable buddhological identification took hold. In the Meiji restoration of 'pure' Shinto she was presented as the foremother of the nation; after 1945 her story returned to the libraries of myth. Folklore studies of the period found her scattered cult strongest in the San'in and Kibi regions, close to the geography the chronicles assign her.
lore.culturalLegacy: Izanami is the most re-imagined figure of the Japanese pantheon: tragic mother in one reading, vengeful corpse-queen in another, and — in modern manga, anime, and games — a glamorous embodiment of death's authority. The drifting Hiruko of the chronicles was later rationalized as Ebisu, the laughing god of fishermen, giving her first failure a strange afterlife as another deity's fortune. Place-names and shrines anchor her legend around Awaji and the Kibi region, and Taga Taisha in Shiga honors the pair. The curse and counter-curse of Yomotsu-hirasaka remain the mythic charter for Japanese funeral grief: the dead take a thousand; the living answer with fifteen hundred.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Izanami is what the creation costs. The chronicle honors her in its way — organ by organ, her dying body is catalogued with the same care as the gods — but it never absolves her of the first error, and it lets her end as the enemy of the living. To read her fairly is to see a deity whom ritual order made the scapegoat: she spoke first, she died of brilliance, and her grief became monstrous only after it was witnessed.

The myth also encodes an unsentimental ecology of reproduction: births outnumber deaths fifteen hundred to a thousand, and the negotiation happens across a stone neither party can move. She is the great refusal at the heart of Japanese cosmology — the door that stays shut, the face that may not be looked upon, the love that must remain on its own side of the rock.
lore.archaeology: Izanami's cult geography clusters where the myth's geography points. Taga Taisha (Shiga Prefecture) venerates the creation pair and preserves the medieval Taga-dera engi recounting her story. On Awaji Island, Izanagi Jingū serves the pair's legend at the traditional site of Onogoroshima. Mount Hiba in the Chūgoku region — named in the Kojiki as her burial place — anchors the myth in real landscape, and the ancient ritual sites around it have been linked to early underworld cult. The Engishiki lists shrines receiving state offerings for Izanami, confirming that by the tenth century the official cult acknowledged the dead goddess alongside the living one.
